body: When life is quiet you train, you eat well and it works, so you know you can do this. Then, sooner or later, {disruption}, and training is the first thing to go.

You don't start again when that week ends. You tell yourself you'll get back to it when things calm down, and then you wait, so a few busy days end up costing you weeks. If things were going to calm down, they would have by now.
It feels like you don't have the time, but the problem is the plan, because every plan you've tried was competing with your schedule, and your schedule always wins.
thisWeek: Don't wait for a good week. I've got a workout that fits into your worst one. It takes ten to fifteen minutes and you don't need a gym.

Do push-ups, then inverted rows, then squats. For the rows, lie under a sturdy table, hold the edge and pull your chest up to it. Take every set close to the point where you can't do another rep, rest a minute and go through it again. If you have the time and the strength left, do a third round. If something's hurting, or you're coming back from being sick, keep every rep pain-free and stop a few reps short.
Do it tomorrow morning, before work. You'll walk in feeling tighter, like a guy who already did something hard today, and you won't want to waste that.

At lunch you'll want a real meal. Start the plate with a good piece of protein, then add vegetables and some slow carbs like rice or potatoes. By dinner you've made good decisions all day, so you don't overeat, and you actually talk with the people at the table.
Next time you pick a plan, ask yourself if it would survive your worst week.
C.headline: You're on track in a calm week, and a busy week stops you every time.
C.name: Fair‑Weather Racer

body: When you're on, you're all in, with training every day, clean food and no drinks, and for a few weeks it works. But the plan only counts when you do all of it, so part of you is already waiting to fail.

Then something small breaks the streak, like a dinner out or a few drinks. One miss feels like the whole thing is ruined, so you write off the rest of the week, and “I'll start again Monday” turns into a month. When you do come back, you come back stricter than the last time.

Going all in is how athletes train, and it works for them because a coach gets them back on track the morning after a bad day. You're doing it the athlete's way with no coach, so after a miss you stay off until you can go all in again. A strict week also makes the miss more likely, because by Friday dinner you're starving.
thisWeek: This one might feel backwards. For the next seven days, eat proper meals throughout the day, every day, including the days you'd usually try to be good. Start every plate with a good piece of protein, and don't save anything up for the weekend.

When you fuel yourself properly all week, you sleep better and you have the energy to train. Then you sit down at the dinner that usually throws you off, rested and not starving. You're in a position to make a good decision for yourself, and to actually talk with the people at the table.
A.headline: You're all in until the first miss, and then you're all out.
A.name: Lost Athlete

body: While it's on, you do everything it asks. You show up, you follow the plan, and it works.
Then the last day comes, and with nothing to answer to, you drift, until you sign up for the next thing and do it all over again.

You call that needing accountability. But someone checking on you only works while they're checking, and when you do something only because there's an end date, you stop when the date passes. You've been on track before, but never once with nobody checking, because it was always someone else's plan and nobody showed you how to make your own.
thisWeek: Think back to the last time you were on track and pick the one or two small things you actually enjoyed back then, the ones that felt like nothing at the time. Maybe it was the breakfast that kept you away from the snacks all morning, or the long walk you took every weekend. Forget everything else and do just those this week.
Keep them small enough that skipping would feel silly. A week from now you'll have stuck to something with nobody checking, only because you wanted to, and no program ever gave you that.
F.headline: You do the work for a challenge, a coach or a date, and you stop when they end.
F.name: Finish Line Chaser

body: You don't stop to eat during the day, and that's what makes you a Pit Stop Dodger. Coffee gets you through the morning, then whatever's closest, if anything, because a proper meal feels like time you don't have. By the evening you're hungry and worn out at once. Dinner goes fast, you go back for more, and later you're in the pantry or pouring a drink without really deciding to.
Every plan you've tried asked you to say no at night, when you're hungry and worn out. When it didn't work you blamed yourself, for something that was decided before 3pm.
thisWeek: Starting tomorrow, eat a bigger lunch every workday and leave everything else as it is. The plate starts with a good piece of protein, then vegetables and some slow carbs like rice or potatoes.

Think of that lunch as an investment in the second half of your day. You get through the afternoon on steady energy, and you sit down to dinner hungry but not starving, with enough left to talk with the people at the table.
E.headline: By 9:30 at night you have nothing left.
E.name: Pit Stop Dodger
